title: A Duck on the Pond

p: A duck has soft feathers under its wings.
Oil on the top feathers keeps the water out.
The soft ones under them stay dry.
So the duck stays warm all day long.
A duck has soft feathers under its wings.
Oil on top keeps the water out.

qs: main idea/detail
What keeps the water out?
Oil on the top feathers keeps the water out.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the soft feathers) and paragraph D (i.e. staying warm).
summarize
Tell what this is about.
A duck has soft feathers under its wings. Oil on the top feathers keeps the water out, so the soft ones stay dry and the duck stays warm.
vocabulary

feathers: what covers a bird.
oil: a slippery stuff that water runs off.
connection
Describe the connection between the oil and the duck staying warm.
Oil on the top feathers keeps the water out, so the soft ones under them stay dry and the duck stays warm.
note: Read it twice. The second time, stop after each paragraph and ask what that one sentence told you.

title: The Crossing Light

p: A white walking man means you may cross.
A red hand means you must wait.
The numbers count down the seconds left.
Look both ways even when the man is white.
A white man means you may cross.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the red hand mean?
A red hand means you must wait.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the numbers) and paragraph D (i.e. looking both ways).
summarize
Tell what the crossing light shows.
A white walking man means you may cross and a red hand means you must wait. The numbers count down the seconds left, and you look both ways even when the man is white.
vocabulary

cross: to walk from one side to the other.
count down: to go backward, like five, four, three.
connection
Describe the connection between the white man and looking both ways.
You look both ways even when the man is white, because the light tells cars to stop but cannot make them.
note: Paragraph D is the one that matters most and it comes last. Say it again at the end.

title: Where a Bear Sleeps

p: A bear finds a cave or a hole in winter.
It sleeps there for many months.
It does not eat the whole time.
In spring it comes out thin and hungry.
A bear finds a cave in winter.
In spring it comes out hungry.

qs: main idea/detail
Where does the bear sleep?
A bear finds a cave or a hole in winter.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. not eating) and paragraph D (i.e. spring).
summarize
Tell what a bear does in winter.
A bear finds a cave or a hole, sleeps there for many months without eating, and comes out thin and hungry in spring.
vocabulary

cave: a hole in rock big enough to go into.
spring: the season that comes after winter.
connection
Describe the connection between not eating and being hungry.
It does not eat the whole time, so in spring it comes out thin and hungry.
note: Four paragraphs, four steps, in order. Count them on your fingers with the child.

title: The School Nurse

p: The nurse has a small room by the office.
She keeps bandages, ice packs and a cot.
She writes down every child who comes in.
She calls home if a child needs to go.
The nurse has a room by the office.
She keeps bandages and ice packs.
She writes down who comes in.
She calls home if you need to go.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the nurse keep?
She keeps bandages, ice packs and a cot.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. writing it down) and paragraph D (i.e. calling home).
summarize
Tell what the school nurse does.
The nurse has a small room by the office with bandages, ice packs and a cot. She writes down every child who comes in, and she calls home if a child needs to go.
vocabulary

bandage: a cover that goes on a cut.
cot: a small bed you can lie down on.
connection
Describe the connection between writing it down and calling home.
She writes down every child who comes in, so she knows who to call home about.
note: Children know this room. Ask what they have seen in it before you read a word.

title: How a Snail Moves

p: A snail has one wide foot under its shell.
It makes slime to slide along.
The slime lets it cross a sharp edge.
You can see the shiny trail it left.
A snail has one foot under its shell.
It makes slime to slide on.
You can see its shiny trail.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the snail make?
It makes slime to slide along.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the sharp edge) and paragraph D (i.e. the trail).
summarize
Tell how a snail moves.
A snail has one wide foot under its shell. It makes slime to slide along, the slime lets it cross a sharp edge, and you can see the shiny trail it left.
vocabulary

slime: wet slippery stuff.
trail: the mark something leaves behind.
connection
Describe the connection between the slime and the trail.
It makes slime to slide along, and you can see the shiny trail it left.
note: Paragraph C is the surprise: the slime is protection, not just slipperiness.

title: Winter Coats

p: A dog grows thicker fur when it gets cold.
The thick fur holds warm air near the skin.
In spring the dog sheds it again.
A coat of fur comes and goes with the year.
A dog grows thicker fur when it is cold.
The fur holds warm air near the skin.
In spring the dog sheds it.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the thick fur hold?
The thick fur holds warm air near the skin.
paragraph focus
Paragraph A (i.e. growing fur) and paragraph C (i.e. shedding it).
summarize
Tell what this is about.
A dog grows thicker fur when it gets cold, and the thick fur holds warm air near the skin. In spring the dog sheds it, so a coat of fur comes and goes with the year.
vocabulary

fur: the hair that covers an animal.
sheds: drops off.
connection
Describe the connection between the cold and the thick fur.
A dog grows thicker fur when it gets cold, and sheds it again in spring.
note: The topic is the whole year, not just winter. Paragraph D is what says so.

title: The Grocery Cart

p: A cart has four wheels and a deep basket.
The two front wheels can turn any way.
That is how you steer around a corner.
The back wheels only roll straight.
A cart has four wheels and a basket.
The front wheels turn any way.

qs: main idea/detail
Which wheels can turn any way?
The two front wheels can turn any way.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. steering) and paragraph D (i.e. the back wheels).
summarize
Tell what this is about.
A cart has four wheels and a deep basket. The two front wheels can turn any way, which is how you steer around a corner, and the back wheels only roll straight.
vocabulary

steer: to make something go the way you want.
basket: the part that holds what you put in.
connection
Describe the connection between the front wheels and steering.
The two front wheels can turn any way, and that is how you steer around a corner.
note: Have the child push a cart and watch the wheels. The text will make sense in one trip.

title: Seeds in the Wind

p: A dandelion seed has a tiny white parachute.
The wind lifts it high off the stem.
It can land far from the plant it came from.
That is how one plant fills a whole yard.
A dandelion seed has a white top.
The wind lifts it off the stem.
That is how a yard fills up.

qs: main idea/detail
What lifts the seed?
The wind lifts it high off the stem.
paragraph focus
Paragraph A (i.e. the parachute) and paragraph D (i.e. filling a yard).
summarize
Tell what this is about.
A dandelion seed has a tiny white parachute. The wind lifts it high off the stem and it can land far from the plant it came from, which is how one plant fills a whole yard.
vocabulary

parachute: a soft top that catches the air.
stem: the part that holds a plant up.
connection
Describe the connection between the parachute and landing far away.
The seed has a tiny white parachute, so the wind lifts it high and it can land far from the plant it came from.
note: Blow a real dandelion if you can. Paragraph D is the part they will remember.

title: The Library Shelf

p: Picture books sit on the low shelves.
The low shelves are where children can reach.
Thick books sit up high for big readers.
Every shelf has a letter on the end.
Picture books sit on the low shelves.
Children can reach the low shelves.

qs: main idea/detail
Where do picture books sit?
Picture books sit on the low shelves.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. reaching) and paragraph D (i.e. the letters).
summarize
Tell what this is about.
Picture books sit on the low shelves where children can reach, thick books sit up high for big readers, and every shelf has a letter on the end.
vocabulary

shelf: a flat board that holds books.
reach: to be able to touch.
connection
Describe the connection between the low shelves and children.
Picture books sit on the low shelves, because the low shelves are where children can reach.
note: Ask the child to find the letter on the end of their own shelf at school.

title: Why Ice Floats

p: Water gets bigger when it turns to ice.
A bigger piece of the same water is lighter.
So ice floats on top instead of sinking.
That is why a pond freezes from the top.
Water gets bigger when it freezes.
A pond freezes from the top down.

qs: main idea/detail
What happens to water when it freezes?
Water gets bigger when it turns to ice.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. floating) and paragraph D (i.e. the pond).
summarize
Tell what this is about.
Water gets bigger when it turns to ice, and a bigger piece of the same water is lighter. So ice floats on top instead of sinking, which is why a pond freezes from the top.
vocabulary

floats: stays up on top of the water.
freezes: turns into ice.
connection
Describe the connection between ice being lighter and a pond freezing on top.
A bigger piece of the same water is lighter, so ice floats on top and a pond freezes from the top down.
note: This one is hard and worth it. Put an ice cube in a glass and watch where it sits.

title: Rain and the Worm

p: Worms live in little tunnels in the dirt.
When it rains hard, the tunnels fill with water.
The worms come up so they can breathe.
That is why you see them on the path.
Worms live in tunnels in the dirt.
Rain fills the tunnels with water.
The worms come up to breathe.
You see them on the path.

qs: main idea/detail
Where do worms live?
Worms live in little tunnels in the dirt.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. the rain) and paragraph C (i.e. coming up).
summarize
Tell what this is about.
Worms live in tunnels in the dirt. When it rains hard the tunnels fill with water, so the worms come up to breathe, and that is why you see them on the path.
vocabulary

tunnel: a hole that goes along under the ground.
breathe: to take in air.
connection
Describe the connection between the rain and the worms on the path.
When it rains hard the tunnels fill with water, so the worms come up so they can breathe and you see them on the path.
note: Go out after rain and look. The child will have the answer before you read a word.

title: The Sun and the Shadow

p: A shadow is made when you block the sun.
In the morning your shadow is very long.
At noon the sun is high and it is short.
The shadow moves all day as the sun moves.
A shadow comes when you block the sun.
In the morning it is long.
It moves as the sun moves.

qs: main idea/detail
When is your shadow long?
In the morning your shadow is very long.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. noon) and paragraph D (i.e. moving all day).
summarize
Tell what this is about.
A shadow is made when you block the sun. In the morning your shadow is very long, at noon the sun is high and it is short, and the shadow moves all day as the sun moves.
vocabulary

shadow: the dark shape you make in the sun.
block: to get in the way of.
connection
Describe the connection between the sun and the shadow's size.
At noon the sun is high and the shadow is short, so the shadow moves and changes all day as the sun moves.
note: Chalk around a shadow in the morning and look again at lunch. The text is the explanation.

title: The Line and the Door

p: Our class makes a line before we go out.
The line keeps everybody together in the hall.
The leader stops at the door and waits.
Then the teacher can count us all.
Our class makes a line to go out.
The leader waits at the door.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the line do?
The line keeps everybody together in the hall.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the leader waiting) and paragraph D (i.e. counting).
summarize
Tell what this is about.
Our class makes a line before we go out. The line keeps everybody together in the hall, the leader stops at the door and waits, and then the teacher can count us all.
vocabulary

leader: the person at the front.
count: to say how many.
connection
Describe the connection between the leader waiting and the teacher counting.
The leader stops at the door and waits, so the teacher can count us all.
note: This is their own routine. Ask what goes wrong when the leader does not wait.

title: The Bird and the Berry

p: A bird eats a red berry off a bush.
The seed inside goes right through the bird.
It lands far away in a new spot.
A new bush can grow from that seed.
A bird eats a red berry.
The seed goes through the bird.
A new bush can grow there.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the bird eat?
A bird eats a red berry off a bush.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. the seed) and paragraph D (i.e. the new bush).
summarize
Tell what this is about.
A bird eats a red berry off a bush. The seed inside goes right through the bird and lands far away in a new spot, and a new bush can grow from that seed.
vocabulary

berry: a small soft fruit.
seed: the part a new plant grows from.
connection
Describe the connection between the bird and the new bush.
The seed goes right through the bird and lands far away, so a new bush can grow from that seed.
note: The bird is doing the plant a favor without meaning to. Say that part out loud.

title: The Bell and the Bus

p: The last bell rings at three o'clock.
The buses are already waiting in a row.
Each bus has a number on the front.
You find your own number and get on.
The last bell rings at three.
The buses wait in a row.
You find your number and get on.

qs: main idea/detail
What is on the front of each bus?
Each bus has a number on the front.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. the buses waiting) and paragraph D (i.e. finding your number).
summarize
Tell what this is about.
The last bell rings at three o'clock, the buses are already waiting in a row, each bus has a number on the front, and you find your own number and get on.
vocabulary

row: a line side by side.
number: a figure like 7 or 12.
connection
Describe the connection between the number and getting on the right bus.
Each bus has a number on the front, so you find your own number and get on.
note: Ask the child their bus number before you read. Then read, and see if they smile.

title: What Shed Means

p: The book says a snake will shed its skin.
Shed means to let something drop off.
The old skin comes off in one long piece.
A new skin was waiting underneath.
The book says a snake will shed its skin.
Shed means to let it drop off.
The old skin comes off whole.
A new skin is under it.

qs: main idea/detail
What does shed mean?
Shed means to let something drop off.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the old skin) and paragraph D (i.e. the new one).
summarize
Tell what shed means.
The book says a snake will shed its skin. Shed means to let something drop off, the old skin comes off in one long piece, and a new skin was waiting underneath.
vocabulary

shed: to let something drop off.
underneath: under something else.
connection
Describe the connection between the old skin and the new one.
The old skin comes off in one long piece, and a new skin was waiting underneath.
note: Paragraph B is the answer and the others are the proof. Ask which sentence gives the meaning.

title: What Recess Means

p: The note says recess is after lunch.
Recess means time outside to play.
You can run, climb or sit with a friend.
A bell ends recess and then you line up.
The note says recess is after lunch.
Recess means time outside to play.

qs: main idea/detail
What does recess mean?
Recess means time outside to play.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. what you can do) and paragraph D (i.e. the bell).
summarize
Tell what recess means.
The note says recess is after lunch. Recess means time outside to play, you can run, climb or sit with a friend, and a bell ends recess and then you line up.
vocabulary

recess: time outside to play.
ends: stops.
connection
Describe the connection between the bell and lining up.
A bell ends recess and then you line up.
note: They live this word every day and may never have been told what it means.

title: What Hatch Means

p: The book says the chick will hatch today.
Hatch means to come out of an egg.
The chick pecks the shell from inside.
It takes many hours and nobody helps it.
The book says the chick will hatch.
Hatch means to come out of an egg.

qs: main idea/detail
What does hatch mean?
Hatch means to come out of an egg.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. pecking) and paragraph D (i.e. no help).
summarize
Tell what hatch means.
The book says the chick will hatch today. Hatch means to come out of an egg, the chick pecks the shell from inside, and it takes many hours and nobody helps it.
vocabulary

hatch: to come out of an egg.
pecks: hits with a beak.
connection
Describe the connection between pecking and hatching.
The chick pecks the shell from inside, which is how it comes out of the egg.
note: Paragraph D is the hard part to hear. Children want to help, and the text says not to.

title: What Line Up Means

p: The teacher says to line up at the door.
Line up means to stand one behind another.
You leave a little space in front of you.
Then the line can walk without bumping.
The teacher says to line up at the door.
Line up means to stand one behind another.
Leave a little space in front.

qs: main idea/detail
What does line up mean?
Line up means to stand one behind another.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the space) and paragraph D (i.e. not bumping).
summarize
Tell what line up means.
The teacher says to line up at the door. Line up means to stand one behind another, you leave a little space in front of you, and then the line can walk without bumping.
vocabulary

line up: to stand one behind another.
space: the gap between two things.
connection
Describe the connection between the space and not bumping.
You leave a little space in front of you, so then the line can walk without bumping.
note: Practice paragraph C with arms out. The space becomes obvious in one try.

title: What Bloom Means

p: The sign says the tulips will bloom in April.
Bloom means to open into a flower.
Before that the bud is closed and green.
After it blooms the petals show their color.
The sign says the tulips will bloom.
Bloom means to open into a flower.
First the bud is closed and green.
Then the petals show their color.

qs: main idea/detail
What does bloom mean?
Bloom means to open into a flower.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the closed bud) and paragraph D (i.e. the petals).
summarize
Tell what bloom means.
The sign says the tulips will bloom in April. Bloom means to open into a flower, before that the bud is closed and green, and after it blooms the petals show their color.
vocabulary

bloom: to open into a flower.
bud: a closed flower before it opens.
connection
Describe the connection between the bud and the petals.
Before it blooms the bud is closed and green, and after it blooms the petals show their color.
note: Before and after is the shape here. Ask which paragraph is before and which is after.

title: The Front of a Book

p: The front cover is the first thing you see.
It has the name of the book on it.
It usually has a big picture too.
The front cover tells you what is inside.
The front cover is what you see first.
It has the name of the book.
It tells you what is inside.

qs: main idea/detail
What is on the front cover?
It has the name of the book on it.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the picture) and paragraph D (i.e. what is inside).
summarize
Tell what the front cover does.
The front cover is the first thing you see. It has the name of the book and usually a big picture, and it tells you what is inside.
vocabulary

cover: the outside of a book.
name: what a thing is called.
connection
Describe the connection between the picture and what is inside.
The front cover usually has a big picture, and the front cover tells you what is inside.
note: Hold a real book. Point at the front cover before you say anything about it.

title: The Back of a Book

p: Turn the book over to find the back cover.
The back often tells you a little about the story.
It can have stars or words from readers.
The price is usually printed down in a corner.
Turn the book over to find the back.
The back tells a little about the story.
It can have words from readers.
The price is in a corner.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the back cover tell you?
The back often tells you a little about the story.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. words from readers) and paragraph D (i.e. the price).
summarize
Tell what the back cover has on it.
Turn the book over to find the back cover. It often tells you a little about the story, it can have stars or words from readers, and the price is usually printed in a corner.
vocabulary

back cover: the outside at the end of a book.
price: how much something costs.
connection
Describe the connection between the front cover and the back cover.
The front cover is the first thing you see, and you turn the book over to find the back cover.
note: Front and back as a pair. Have the child flip a book over and name each one.

title: The Title Page

p: Open the cover and turn one or two pages.
The title page says the name of the book again.
It also says who wrote it and who drew it.
The front cover is outside and this page is inside.
Open the cover and turn a page.
The title page says the name again.
It says who wrote it and who drew it.
The cover is outside and this is inside.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the title page say?
The title page says the name of the book again.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. who wrote and drew it) and paragraph D (i.e. inside and outside).
summarize
Tell what the title page is.
Open the cover and turn one or two pages to find the title page. It says the name of the book again and who wrote it and who drew it. The front cover is outside and the title page is inside.
vocabulary

title: the name of a book.
title page: the page inside that gives the name again.
connection
Describe the connection between the front cover and the title page.
The front cover is outside and this page is inside, and both of them say the name of the book.
note: The repeat confuses children. Say plainly that the name appears twice on purpose.

title: Which Way Is Up

p: A book has a top and a bottom.
The words go the right way up when you hold it right.
The spine stays on your left as you read.
Turn pages from the right to the left.
A book has a top and a bottom.
Hold it so the words are the right way up.
The spine stays on your left.

qs: main idea/detail
Where does the spine stay?
The spine stays on your left as you read.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. the words the right way up) and paragraph D (i.e. turning pages).
summarize
Tell how to hold a book.
A book has a top and a bottom. You hold it so the words go the right way up, the spine stays on your left as you read, and you turn pages from the right to the left.
vocabulary

spine: the folded edge where a book is held together.
turn: to move a page over.
connection
Describe the connection between the spine and turning pages.
The spine stays on your left as you read, so you turn pages from the right to the left.
note: Do it with them rather than telling them. Hand over a book upside down and wait.

title: The Spine of a Book

p: The spine is the folded edge of a book.
It holds all the pages together.
The name is printed down the spine.
That is how you find a book on a shelf.
The spine is the folded edge.
The name is printed on it.
That is how you find it on a shelf.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the spine hold?
It holds all the pages together.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the printed name) and paragraph D (i.e. finding it on a shelf).
summarize
Tell what the spine of a book is.
The spine is the folded edge of a book. It holds all the pages together, the name is printed down the spine, and that is how you find a book on a shelf.
vocabulary

spine: the folded edge that holds a book together.
shelf: a flat board that holds books.
connection
Describe the connection between the name on the spine and finding a book.
The name is printed down the spine, and that is how you find a book on a shelf.
note: Stand a book on a shelf and ask what you can still see. Only the spine.

title: Who Wrote It

p: The author is the person who wrote the words.
The author decides what the book will tell you.
You can find the name on the front cover.
The same author may write many books.
The author decides what the book says.
The name is on the front cover.
One author can write many books.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the author do?
The author is the person who wrote the words.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. deciding what the book tells you) and paragraph D (i.e. many books).
summarize
Tell what an author does.
The author is the person who wrote the words and decides what the book will tell you. You can find the name on the front cover, and the same author may write many books.
vocabulary

author: the person who wrote the words.
decides: picks what will happen.
connection
Describe the connection between the author and what the book tells you.
The author is the person who wrote the words, and the author decides what the book will tell you.
note: Say author, not writer, every time. The word itself is the point of this standard.

title: Who Drew It

p: The illustrator is the person who made the pictures.
The illustrator decides what everything looks like.
Their name is on the cover under the author's.
A book can have pictures and no story.
The illustrator decides how things look.
Their name is under the author's.
A book can be all pictures.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the illustrator do?
The illustrator is the person who made the pictures.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. deciding how things look) and paragraph C (i.e. where the name sits).
summarize
Tell what an illustrator does.
The illustrator is the person who made the pictures and decides what everything looks like. Their name is on the cover under the author's name.
vocabulary

illustrator: the person who made the pictures.
looks like: how a thing appears.
connection
Describe the connection between the illustrator and the pictures.
The illustrator is the person who made the pictures, and decides what everything looks like.
note: Pair this with Who Wrote It. The two words are easier side by side than alone.

title: Two Names on One Book

p: Many books have two different names on the front cover.
One of them wrote all the words.
The other one drew all the pictures.
They worked on the same book together.
Many books have two names on the cover.
They worked on the same book.

qs: main idea/detail
How many names are on the cover?
Many books have two different names on the front cover.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. the words) and paragraph C (i.e. the pictures).
summarize
Tell why a book has two names.
Many books have two different names on the front cover. One of them wrote all the words and the other one drew all the pictures, and they worked on the same book together.
vocabulary

cover: the outside of a book.
together: with each other.
connection
Describe the connection between the two names.
One of them wrote all the words and the other drew all the pictures, and they worked on the same book together.
note: Hold up a book with two names and ask the child to guess which one did which.

title: When One Person Does Both

p: Some books have only one name on them.
That person wrote the words and drew the pictures.
They are the author and the illustrator.
That one person did both of the jobs.
Some books have only one name.
That person wrote the words and drew the pictures.
They are the author and the illustrator.

qs: main idea/detail
What did that one person do?
That person wrote the words and drew the pictures.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. being both) and paragraph D (i.e. both jobs).
summarize
Tell what it means when a book has one name.
Some books have only one name on them. That person wrote the words and drew the pictures, so they are the author and the illustrator, and one person did both of the jobs.
vocabulary

both: the two of them.
job: work that somebody does.
connection
Describe the connection between the one name and the two jobs.
Some books have only one name because that person wrote the words and drew the pictures, so one person did both of the jobs.
note: This is the hard case and it comes fourth on purpose. Do the two-name books first.

title: Where to Find the Names

p: Look at the front cover for the names.
Look at the title page inside for them too.
The author's name is usually on top.
The illustrator's name is usually under it.
Look at the front cover for the names.
Look at the title page too.
The author is usually on top.

qs: main idea/detail
Where can you find the names?
Look at the front cover for the names, and look at the title page inside for them too.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the author on top) and paragraph D (i.e. the illustrator under).
summarize
Tell where the names are.
Look at the front cover for the names and at the title page inside for them too. The author's name is usually on top and the illustrator's name is usually under it.
vocabulary

title page: the page inside that gives the name of the book.
under: below something else.
connection
Describe the connection between the front cover and the title page.
Look at the front cover for the names, and look at the title page inside for them too.
note: Two places, the same two names. Check both on a real book.

title: The Picture Helps the Words

p: The words say that the dog is wet.
The picture shows water dripping off its ears.
Now you know just how wet it is.
The picture and the words work together.
The words say the dog is wet.
The picture shows water dripping off.
Now you know how wet it is.

qs: main idea/detail
What do the words say?
The words say that the dog is wet.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. the dripping water) and paragraph D (i.e. working together).
summarize
Tell how the picture helps the words.
The words say the dog is wet and the picture shows water dripping off its ears, so now you know just how wet it is. The picture and the words work together.
vocabulary

dripping: falling in drops.
together: with each other.
connection
Describe the connection between the words and the picture.
The words say the dog is wet and the picture shows water dripping off its ears, so they work together.
note: Read the words with the picture covered, then uncover it. Ask what changed.

title: Count What You See

p: The words say there are some eggs in a nest.
The picture lets you count them one by one.
There are four eggs in that nest.
The picture gave you the number.
The words say there are some eggs.
The picture lets you count them.

qs: main idea/detail
How many eggs are there?
There are four eggs in that nest.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. counting) and paragraph D (i.e. the number).
summarize
Tell how the picture helped.
The words say there are some eggs in a nest. The picture lets you count them one by one, there are four eggs, and the picture gave you the number.
vocabulary

count: to say how many.
nest: the home a bird builds for eggs.
connection
Describe the connection between the word some and the number four.
The words say there are some eggs, and the picture lets you count them and find four.
note: Some is a vague word and children accept it. The picture is what makes it exact.

title: The Picture Shows the Size

p: The words say that a blue whale is big.
The picture puts a bus beside the whale.
The whale is longer than three buses.
Now the word big means something real.
The words say a blue whale is big.
The picture puts a bus beside it.
The whale is longer than three buses.

qs: main idea/detail
What is beside the whale in the picture?
The picture puts a bus beside the whale.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. three buses) and paragraph D (i.e. what big means).
summarize
Tell how the picture shows size.
The words say a blue whale is big. The picture puts a bus beside the whale, the whale is longer than three buses, and now the word big means something real.
vocabulary

size: how big or small a thing is.
beside: next to.
connection
Describe the connection between the bus and the word big.
The picture puts a bus beside the whale so you can see it is longer than three buses, and now the word big means something real.
note: Big is a word children use for everything. The bus is what gives it an amount.

title: What the Words Add

p: The picture shows a frog on a leaf.
You cannot tell if the frog is poisonous.
The words say do not touch this one.
Only the words could tell you that.
The picture shows a frog on a leaf.
You cannot tell if it is poisonous.
The words say do not touch it.
Only the words tell you that.

qs: main idea/detail
What do the words say?
The words say do not touch this one.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. what you cannot tell) and paragraph D (i.e. only the words).
summarize
Tell what the words add to the picture.
The picture shows a frog on a leaf, but you cannot tell if the frog is poisonous. The words say do not touch this one, and only the words could tell you that.
vocabulary

poisonous: able to make you sick if you touch or eat it.
touch: to put a hand on.
connection
Describe the connection between the picture and the warning.
The picture shows a frog on a leaf but cannot tell you if it is poisonous, so only the words could tell you not to touch it.
note: Danger is a thing a picture cannot carry. That is worth saying plainly.

title: A Picture on Every Page

p: This book has a picture on every page.
Each picture shows what that page says.
If you get lost, look at the picture.
The picture will remind you where you are.
This book has a picture on every page.
Each picture shows what the page says.
If you get lost, look at it.
It reminds you where you are.

qs: main idea/detail
What does each picture show?
Each picture shows what that page says.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. getting lost) and paragraph D (i.e. being reminded).
summarize
Tell what the pictures do in this book.
This book has a picture on every page and each one shows what that page says. If you get lost, look at the picture, and it will remind you where you are.
vocabulary

remind: to help you remember.
lost: not sure where you are.
connection
Describe the connection between getting lost and the picture.
If you get lost, look at the picture, and the picture will remind you where you are.
note: This is a strategy, not a fact. Tell the child to try it the next time they get stuck.

title: Why We Wear a Helmet

p: You should wear a helmet on a bike.
One reason is that a fall can hurt your head.
Another reason is that a helmet is soft inside.
It takes the bump instead of you.
Wear a helmet on a bike.
One reason is a fall can hurt your head.
Another is that a helmet is soft inside.
It takes the bump for you.

qs: main idea/detail
What is one reason to wear a helmet?
One reason is that a fall can hurt your head.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the soft inside) and paragraph D (i.e. taking the bump).
summarize
Tell why you wear a helmet.
You should wear a helmet on a bike. One reason is that a fall can hurt your head, and another is that a helmet is soft inside, so it takes the bump instead of you.
vocabulary

helmet: a hard hat that keeps your head safe.
reason: why somebody says to do a thing.
connection
Describe the connection between the soft inside and your head.
A helmet is soft inside, so it takes the bump instead of you.
note: Two reasons, in B and C. Hold up two fingers while you read them.

title: Why Plants Need Rain

p: A plant will die without any rain.
One reason is that roots drink the water.
Another reason is that water carries food up.
A dry plant droops and then turns brown.
A plant will die without rain.
One reason is that roots drink water.
Another is that water carries food up.

qs: main idea/detail
What do the roots do?
One reason is that roots drink the water.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. carrying food) and paragraph D (i.e. the dry plant).
summarize
Tell why plants need rain.
A plant will die without any rain. One reason is that roots drink the water, and another is that water carries food up. A dry plant droops and then turns brown.
vocabulary

roots: the parts of a plant under the ground.
droops: hangs down instead of standing up.
connection
Describe the connection between no rain and a brown plant.
Roots drink the water and water carries food up, so a dry plant droops and then turns brown.
note: Paragraph D is the proof for both reasons. Ask what happens if neither one happens.

title: Why We Hold the Rail

p: Hold the rail on the stairs every time.
One reason is that stairs are easy to trip on.
Another reason is that the rail catches you.
Your hand is already there if you slip.
Hold the rail on the stairs.
One reason is that stairs are easy to trip on.
Another is that the rail catches you.

qs: main idea/detail
What is one reason to hold the rail?
One reason is that stairs are easy to trip on.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the rail catching you) and paragraph D (i.e. your hand already there).
summarize
Tell why you hold the rail.
Hold the rail on the stairs every time. One reason is that stairs are easy to trip on, and another is that the rail catches you, because your hand is already there if you slip.
vocabulary

rail: the bar beside the stairs that you hold.
trip: to catch your foot and fall.
connection
Describe the connection between holding the rail and slipping.
Your hand is already there if you slip, so the rail catches you.
note: Paragraph D is the real reason: already there beats grabbing late. Say it that way.

title: Why Birds Fly South

p: Many birds fly south before winter comes.
One reason is that the bugs are gone up here.
Another reason is that water freezes over.
They go where food is still easy to find.
Many birds fly south before winter.
One reason is that the bugs are gone.
They go where food is easy to find.

qs: main idea/detail
What is one reason birds fly south?
One reason is that the bugs are gone up here.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. the frozen water) and paragraph D (i.e. finding food).
summarize
Tell why birds fly south.
Many birds fly south before winter comes. One reason is that the bugs are gone up here, and another is that water freezes over, so they go where food is still easy to find.
vocabulary

south: the warm way, down on a map.
freezes: turns to ice.
connection
Describe the connection between the two reasons and the food.
The bugs are gone and the water freezes over, so the birds go where food is still easy to find.
note: Both reasons are about food. Paragraph D is the one that names that.

title: Why We Share the Blocks

p: Everybody shares the blocks in our room.
One reason is that there is only one set.
Another reason is that two can build more.
A big tower needs more hands than one.
One reason is there is only one set.
Another is that two can build more.
A big tower needs more hands.

qs: main idea/detail
What is one reason to share?
One reason is that there is only one set.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. two building more) and paragraph D (i.e. the big tower).
summarize
Tell why the class shares the blocks.
Everybody shares the blocks because there is only one set, and because two can build more than one. A big tower needs more hands than one.
vocabulary

share: to let others use it too.
set: all of one thing kept together.
connection
Describe the connection between two children and a big tower.
Two can build more, because a big tower needs more hands than one.
note: Paragraph B is a rule and paragraph C is a benefit. Ask which reason they like better.

title: Two Books About Cats

p: Both of these books are about cats.
One book is about a pet cat at home.
The other is about big cats in the wild.
Both books say cats sleep a lot.
One is about a pet cat.
The other is about big wild cats.
Both say cats sleep a lot.

qs: main idea/detail
What do both books say?
Both books say cats sleep a lot.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. the pet cat) and paragraph C (i.e. the wild cats).
summarize
Tell how the two cat books are alike and different.
Both books are about cats and both say cats sleep a lot. One is about a pet cat at home and the other is about big cats in the wild.
vocabulary

pet: an animal that lives with people.
wild: living out in nature, not with people.
connection
Describe the connection between the two books.
Both books are about cats and both say cats sleep a lot, but one is a pet and the others are wild.
note: Same and different. Say the same part first, every time.

title: Two Books About Trucks

p: Both of these two books are about trucks.
One book shows a fire truck up close.
The other one shows every kind of truck.
Both books have big photos on each page.
Both of these books are about trucks.
One book shows a fire truck.
The other shows many kinds of truck.

qs: main idea/detail
What do both books have?
Both books have big photos on each page.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. the fire truck) and paragraph C (i.e. every kind).
summarize
Tell how the two truck books are alike and different.
Both books are about trucks and both have big photos on each page. One shows a fire truck up close and the other shows every kind of truck.
vocabulary

photo: a picture made with a camera.
kind: a sort or type of thing.
connection
Describe the connection between the two books.
Both books are about trucks with big photos, but one is about a single fire truck and the other is about every kind.
note: One book goes deep and one goes wide. Ask which they would pick to learn about a fire truck.

title: Two Books About Apples

p: Both books are about apples in the fall.
One book shows how an apple grows.
The other shows how to bake a pie.
Both of the books start with a tree.
One shows how an apple grows.
The other shows how to bake a pie.

qs: main idea/detail
What do both books start with?
Both of the books start with a tree.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. growing) and paragraph C (i.e. baking).
summarize
Tell how the two apple books are alike and different.
Both books are about apples in the fall and both start with a tree. One shows how an apple grows and the other shows how to bake a pie.
vocabulary

bake: to cook in an oven.
fall: the season when leaves drop.
connection
Describe the connection between the two books.
Both books start with a tree, but one follows the apple on the tree and the other follows it into a pie.
note: Same beginning, two endings. Draw the fork in the road with your finger.

title: Two Books About the Moon

p: Both of these books are about the moon.
One book shows the moon changing shape.
The other shows people landing on it.
Both books have a big photo of the full moon.
Both books are about the moon.
One shows the moon changing shape.
The other shows people landing on it.
Both have a photo of the full moon.

qs: main idea/detail
What do both books have?
Both books have a big photo of the full moon.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. changing shape) and paragraph C (i.e. landing on it).
summarize
Tell how the two moon books are alike and different.
Both books are about the moon and both have a photo of the full moon. One shows the moon changing shape and the other shows people landing on it.
vocabulary

full moon: the moon when it looks like a whole circle.
landing: coming down onto something.
connection
Describe the connection between the two books.
Both books are about the moon and both show the full moon, but one is about its shape and one is about people going there.
note: One is about the sky and one is about people. That split comes up again and again.

title: Two Books About Bugs

p: Both of these books are about bugs in the yard.
One book is only about ants.
The other has a page for each bug.
Both books tell you how many legs.
One book is only about ants.
The other has a page for each bug.
Both tell you how many legs.

qs: main idea/detail
What do both books tell you?
Both books tell you how many legs.
paragraph focus
Paragraph B (i.e. only ants) and paragraph C (i.e. a page each).
summarize
Tell how the two bug books are alike and different.
Both books are about bugs in the yard and both tell you how many legs. One is only about ants and the other has a page for each bug.
vocabulary

legs: the parts an animal walks on.
page: one side of a sheet in a book.
connection
Describe the connection between the two books.
Both books tell you how many legs a bug has, but one is only about ants and the other covers many bugs.
note: Ask which book you would open to find out about a beetle.

title: Reading Together on the Rug

p: The class sits on the rug to read together.
Everybody can see the big book from there.
You listen while the teacher reads a page.
Then everybody talks about that page.
The class sits on the rug to read.
Everybody can see the big book.
You listen while the teacher reads.

qs: main idea/detail
Where does the class sit?
The class sits on the rug to read together.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. listening) and paragraph D (i.e. talking).
summarize
Tell what reading together looks like.
The class sits on the rug so everybody can see the big book. You listen while the teacher reads a page, and then everybody talks about that page.
vocabulary

together: all at the same time.
listen: to pay attention with your ears.
connection
Describe the connection between listening and talking.
You listen while the teacher reads a page, and then everybody talks about that page.
note: Listen, then talk, is the whole routine. Say the order out loud before you start.

title: When to Ask Your Question

p: You will have questions while we read together.
Hold the question until the page is done.
Then put your hand up and ask it.
That way nobody misses the next part.
You will have questions while we read.
Hold the question until the page is done.
That way nobody misses the next part.

qs: main idea/detail
What do you do with your question?
Hold the question until the page is done.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. putting your hand up) and paragraph D (i.e. not missing the next part).
summarize
Tell when to ask a question.
You will have questions while we read. Hold the question until the page is done, then put your hand up and ask it, so nobody misses the next part.
vocabulary

question: something you want to find out.
hold: to keep for a little while.
connection
Describe the connection between waiting and not missing anything.
Hold the question until the page is done, and that way nobody misses the next part.
note: Children think waiting means their question does not matter. Paragraph D says why it does.

title: Looking Where the Reader Points

p: The teacher points at the words while reading.
Your eyes follow the finger across the page.
That shows you which word is being said.
The words always go from left to right.
The teacher points at the words.
That shows which word is said.
The words go from left to right.

qs: main idea/detail
What do your eyes follow?
Your eyes follow the finger across the page.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. which word is being said) and paragraph D (i.e. left to right).
summarize
Tell what the pointing finger does.
The teacher points at the words while reading, and your eyes follow the finger across the page. That shows you which word is being said, and the words always go from left to right.
vocabulary

follow: to go along behind.
left to right: the way words go on a page.
connection
Describe the connection between the finger and knowing the word.
Your eyes follow the finger across the page, and that shows you which word is being said.
note: This one is about print awareness. Point slowly and let them watch the finger, not you.

title: Saying What You Noticed

p: After a page, the teacher asks what you noticed.
You can say anything you really saw or heard.
There is more than one right answer.
Somebody else may have noticed something new.
The teacher asks what you noticed.
Say anything you really saw or heard.
There is more than one right answer.

qs: main idea/detail
What does the teacher ask?
After a page, the teacher asks what you noticed.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. more than one right answer) and paragraph D (i.e. somebody else).
summarize
Tell what happens after a page.
After a page, the teacher asks what you noticed. You can say anything you really saw or heard, there is more than one right answer, and somebody else may have noticed something new.
vocabulary

noticed: saw or heard and thought about.
answer: what you say back.
connection
Describe the connection between many answers and listening to others.
There is more than one right answer, so somebody else may have noticed something new.
note: Paragraph C is the one that frees a shy child. Read it twice on the first day.

title: Reading It Again Tomorrow

p: We will read this same book again tomorrow.
The second time you hear more than the first.
You already know what is going to happen.
So your head is free to notice other things.
We will read this book again tomorrow.
The second time you hear more.
So you can notice other things.

qs: main idea/detail
When will the class read the book again?
We will read this same book again tomorrow.
paragraph focus
Paragraph C (i.e. already knowing) and paragraph D (i.e. noticing other things).
summarize
Tell why the class reads a book twice.
The class reads the same book again tomorrow. The second time you hear more than the first, because you already know what is going to happen, so your head is free to notice other things.
vocabulary

second: the one that comes after the first.
free: not busy with something else.
connection
Describe the connection between knowing the story and noticing more.
You already know what is going to happen, so your head is free to notice other things.
note: This explains rereading, which children often take as a punishment. It is the opposite.
